title: Inflammatory Response and Wound Healing Process
introduction: The inflammatory response is the body's sequential, nonspecific vascular and cellular reaction to tissue injury designed to dilute and neutralize injurious agents before adaptive immunity is fully established[cite: 412]. Closely linked to inflammation, wound healing encompasses the structured biological sequence from initial injury to complete wound closure and scar organization—a process that may continue for up to 18 months after closure[cite: 437].
learningOutcomes: 3.1 Differentiate inflammation from infection, identify the six primary signs of inflammation, and classify acute, sub-acute, and chronic inflammation[cite: 412, 413, 419, 420].

3.2 Trace the four stages of the inflammatory response, including vascular changes, cellular mobilization, white blood cell roles, complement activation, arachidonic acid metabolites, and exudate types[cite: 414, 415, 416, 417, 418].
3.3 Distinguish regeneration (labile, stable, and permanent cells) from repair, and apply the RICE nursing interventions to manage inflammation safely[cite: 419, 420].
3.4 Define wound healing, differentiate acute, chronic, and recalcitrant wounds, and classify wounds by underlying cause including surgical incision categories[cite: 437, 438, 439, 440].
3.5 Explain the VIPER mnemonic, the four phases of acute wound healing, biochemical and clinical differences in chronic wounds, and factors that delay wound healing[cite: 441, 442, 443, 444].

content.heading: Inflammation vs. Infection, Cardinal Signs, and Vascular-Cellular Stages
content.body: Although their clinical features overlap, inflammation and infection are not synonymous: infection is the invasion and multiplication of pathogenic biological agents (bacteria, viruses, fungi) in body tissues causing cellular injury, whereas inflammation is a sequential, nonspecific tissue and vascular reaction to cell injury that may also be triggered by non-biological agents such as heat, radiation, trauma, or allergens[cite: 412, 413]. The six primary signs of inflammation are redness (erythema from increased blood flow), heat (from increased metabolism and blood flow), pain (from increased pressure on local pain receptors), swelling (from interstitial fluid and leukocyte accumulation), loss of function (due to pain and swelling), and pus (purulent exudate when infection is present)[cite: 413]. Inflammation progresses through four stages: vascular response, cellular response, exudate formation, and healing[cite: 414]. During the immediate vascular response, transient arteriolar vasoconstriction gives way to vasodilation, hyperaemia, and increased capillary permeability driven by histamine and other mediators; protein-rich fluid shifts into the interstitium (causing edema), while fibrinogen activates into fibrin to reinforce platelet clots and trap bacteria[cite: 414]. During the cellular response, slowed, more viscous blood flow enables neutrophils and monocytes to reach the injury site via margination (moving to the inner capillary wall), diapedesis (amoeboid passage through the capillary wall), and chemotaxis (directional migration along a chemotactic chemical gradient)[cite: 414, 415].

content.heading: White Blood Cells, Complement Cascade, and Inflammatory Mediators
content.body: Five white blood cell groups perform specialized roles during inflammation[cite: 415]. Neutrophils arrive first within 90 minutes to initiate phagocytosis; because they live only 24–48 hours, acute bacterial infection triggers the bone marrow to release immature neutrophils ('bands') alongside mature 'segmented' neutrophils—an increase known as a 'shift to the left'[cite: 415]. Monocytes arrive second within 3–7 days, transform into tissue macrophages to clean the site for healing, and can fuse into longer-lived multinucleated giant cells that form collagen-encapsulated granulomas (such as around the tubercle bacillus)[cite: 415, 416]. Lymphocytes arrive last to initiate humoral and cell-mediated immunity, eosinophils rise in allergies and parasitic infections to modulate histamine/serotonin and phagocytose allergen-antibody complexes, and basophils bind IgE to release histamine and heparin from their granules[cite: 416]. Key chemical mediators include histamine, serotonin, kinins (bradykinin), prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines, and the complement system—at least 20 liver-produced plasma proteins activated sequentially as C1, C4, C2, C3, C5, C6, C7, C8, and C9[cite: 416, 417]. Complement is activated via the Classical pathway (IgG or IgM antigen-antibody complexes fixing C1) or Alternate pathway (bacterial endotoxins starting at C3 through C9) to mediate cellular lysis (requiring full C1–C9 activation, with C8–C9 causing cell rupture), opsonization (C3b), increased permeability, chemotaxis (C5a), anaphylatoxin-triggered histamine release (C3a, C4a, C5a), agglutination, and viral neutralization[cite: 417, 418]. Membrane phospholipid arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon unsaturated fatty acid) yields inflammatory prostaglandins (PGD2, PGE2, PGF2, PGI2) via the cyclooxygenase pathway and leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD, LTE—known as slow-reacting substances of anaphylaxis, SRS-A, causing sustained bronchoconstriction in asthma and anaphylaxis) via the lipoxygenase pathway[cite: 418].

content.heading: Exudates, Inflammation Types, Healing Modes, and RICE Nursing Care
content.body: Exudate formation reflects the injured tissue and duration of inflammation: serous exudate (low cell/protein fluid resembling serum, e.g., blisters and pleural effusion), catarrhal exudate (from mucoid cells in runny nose or upper respiratory infections), fibrinous exudate (excessive fibrin leakage causing tissue adhesions), purulent exudate (pus containing leukocytes, microbes, and dead tissue in boils, abscesses, or cellulitis), and haemorrhagic exudate (from vessel wall rupture/necrosis, such as a haematoma)[cite: 418]. Clinically, acute inflammation heals in 2–3 weeks without residual damage, sub-acute inflammation retains acute features for longer (e.g., infective endocarditis), and chronic inflammation persists for months or years with tissue destruction (e.g., tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis)[cite: 419, 420]. The final healing phase occurs by regeneration (replacing lost cells with identical cells—rapid in constantly dividing labile cells like skin, bone marrow, and lymphoid tissue; injury-triggered in stable cells like liver, pancreas, and kidney; and impossible in non-dividing permanent cells like neurons and skeletal or cardiac muscle) or by repair (connective tissue scar formation via primary, secondary, or tertiary intention)[cite: 419]. Supportive nursing care follows the RICE acronym: Rest (prevents disruption of forming fibrin and collagen), Ice within the first few hours (vasoconstricts to limit swelling, pain, and congestion) followed later by Heat (vasodilates to clear waste products and uses warm moist heat to assist necrotic tissue debridement), Compression (controls bleeding and counters edema, requiring close monitoring of distal pulses and capillary refill to avoid compromised circulation), and Elevation above heart level (enhances venous/lymphatic return to reduce edema and engorgement pain, though elevation must be avoided in patients with significantly reduced arterial circulation)[cite: 420].

content.heading: Wound Types and Etiologic Classifications
content.body: A wound is a disruption of the normal structure and function of the integument or a break in skin and soft tissue continuity[cite: 437]. Based on healing course and duration, wounds are grouped into three types: Acute wounds (commonly traumatic or surgical, progressing through healing in a timely, uncomplicated manner), Chronic wounds (complex wounds caused by pressure, poor circulation, malnutrition, or diabetes that fail to follow orderly repair—marked by prolonged inflammation, cellular senescence, deficient growth factor receptor sites, and elevated proteases), and Recalcitrant wounds (stubborn, refractory, non-healing wounds that remain static with no progress or deteriorate via active tissue destruction)[cite: 438]. By underlying cause, wounds are classified into nine categories: arterial ulcers (limb ischemia from arterial insufficiency), burns (chemical, radiation, electrical, or thermal), diabetic foot ulcers (plantar wounds from trauma, pressure, neuropathy, arterial disease, and infection), incontinence wounds (urinary/faecal skin damage distinct from pressure ulcers), neuropathic ulcers (partial-to-full-thickness loss from peripheral neuropathy not exclusive to diabetes), pressure ulcers (staged I–IV by tissue depth due to unrelieved pressure, shear, or friction), skin graft donor sites (usually partial-thickness surgical sites), vasculitic ulcers (accompanying rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, or Sjogren's syndrome, risking cutaneous infarcts and gangrene), and intentional surgical incisions—subdivided into Clean (minimal endogenous bacterial contamination), Clean-contaminated (possible endogenous contamination), Contaminated (contamination present), and Dirty (infected tissue such as abscesses)[cite: 439, 440].

content.heading: Phases of Acute Wound Healing (VIPER)
content.body: Acute wound healing follows a structured sequence summarized by the mnemonic VIPER—Vascular phase (initial vasoconstriction, platelet activation, rapid fibrin plugging), Inflammatory phase (phagocyte, complement, and antibody mobilization), Proliferative phase (overlapping inflammation to build granulation substrate), Establishment of a new skin barrier, and Remodelling[cite: 441]. Specifically, four biological phases govern acute healing[cite: 441]: (1) Haemostasis—blood contacts extracellular matrix components, platelets aggregate and degranulate, Factor XII (Hageman factor) activates clotting, and subsequent fibrinolysis lets cells migrate into the wound[cite: 441]; (2) Acute Inflammatory Phase (3–4 days)—vasodilation and permeability activate complement, neutrophils peak at 24–48 hours and decline after 3 days if uninfected, followed by macrophages (secreting cytokines, growth factors, and proteolytic enzymes) and lymphocytes, alongside early granulation (fibroblasts, angioblast capillary sprouts, WBCs, exudate, and ground substance)—though necrotic tissue or bacteria trigger abnormal metalloproteases that disrupt cytokines[cite: 441, 442]; (3) Proliferative Phase—fibroblasts deposit collagen for tensile strength, creating pink, vascular, friable granulation tissue that resists infection yet risks dehiscence, while epithelialization migrates surface epithelium across the wound (taking 3–4 days in superficial wounds)[cite: 442]; and (4) Acute Remodelling—the longest, final phase, where myofibroblasts contract the wound edges, fibroblasts disappear, and collagen fibers reorganize into a mature scar that takes about 180 days to resemble normal collagen morphology and regains approximately 80% of unwounded skin's tensile strength[cite: 442].

content.heading: Chronic Wound Pathophysiology and Factors Delaying Healing
content.body: Prolonged or absent inflammation in chronic wounds signals impaired immunity and frequently occurs with diabetes, excessive antiseptic use, radiation therapy, or severe ischemia[cite: 443]. Chronic wounds stall across four dysfunctional phases: Chronic Inflammation (lasting weeks to months with reflex hyperaemia and impaired phagocytosis of necrotic debris), Chronic Proliferation (infection halts progression for up to 11 months), Chronic Epithelialization (stacked cells form rolled, thick, fibrotic wound edges with hyperkeratosis—overgrowth of the horny layer), and Chronic Remodelling (keloid scarring or absent remodelling from intrinsic, extrinsic, or iatrogenic causes preventing scar closure)[cite: 444]. Biochemically, acute wounds feature low inflammatory cytokines, low matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), high cell mitosis, elevated growth factors, and rapid cell response, whereas chronic wounds exhibit high inflammatory cytokines, high MMPs, low cell mitosis, decreased growth factor response, and senescent cells[cite: 444]. Six key clinical factors delay wound healing: local tissue ischemia and neuropathy, tissue necrosis and infection, uncontrolled periwound edema, wound instability, malnutrition, and poor venous return[cite: 444].

inTextQuestions.question: What does a 'shift to the left' in a patient's white blood cell count indicate, and which cell type is responsible?
inTextQuestions.answer: A 'shift to the left' indicates an increased number of immature neutrophils (called bands) released from the bone marrow into circulation to meet high demand, which is common in acute bacterial infections[cite: 415].

inTextQuestions.question: Which type of inflammatory exudate involves mucoid cells, such as in a runny nose or upper respiratory tract infection?
Under the surgical incision classification, when is a surgical wound categorized as 'Dirty'?
inTextQuestions.answer: When infected tissue is present, such as abscesses[cite: 440].

inTextQuestions.question: Approximately what percentage of unwounded skin's tensile strength does a fully healed scar regain, and how long does collagen morphology take to resemble normal skin?
inTextQuestions.answer: A healed wound regains approximately 80% of unwounded skin's tensile strength, and it takes about 180 days for collagen fibre diameter and morphology to regain the appearance of normal skin[cite: 442].

saqs.question: Differentiate between infection and inflammation, and list the six primary signs of inflammation along with their underlying cause.
saqs.answer: Infection is the invasion and multiplication of pathogenic microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi) causing cellular injury, whereas inflammation is a sequential, nonspecific body reaction to cellular injury that can also be caused by non-biological agents like heat, radiation, trauma, or allergens[cite: 412, 422]. The six signs are redness (increased blood flow), heat (increased metabolism and blood flow), pain (pressure on local pain receptors), swelling (interstitial fluid and leukocyte accumulation), loss of function (pain and swelling), and pus (purulent exudate from infection)[cite: 413, 422].

saqs.question: Compare the Classical and Alternate pathways of complement activation and list four biological functions of the complement system.
saqs.answer: The Classical pathway is triggered when IgG or IgM antigen-antibody complexes fix C1, whereas the Alternate pathway is initiated by bacterial endotoxins starting at C3 and proceeding from C5 through C9[cite: 417]. Four functions of the complement system are cellular lysis (C1–C9), opsonization (C3b), chemotaxis (C5a), and increased cell permeability, agglutination, or viral neutralization[cite: 417, 418].

saqs.question: Explain the RICE nursing interventions used to manage inflammation, noting one key safety precaution each for compression and elevation.
saqs.answer: Rest limits activity so fibrin and collagen can bridge wound edges undisturbed; Ice is applied in the first few hours for vasoconstriction to reduce swelling and pain, followed later by Heat to vasodilate and remove wastes; Compression controls bleeding and counters edema; and Elevation above heart level promotes venous and lymphatic return[cite: 420]. Safety precautions: during compression, nurses must assess distal pulses and capillary refill to avoid compromised circulation; elevation must be avoided in patients with significantly reduced arterial circulation[cite: 420].

saqs.question: List and briefly describe the four phases of acute wound healing.
saqs.answer: 1. Haemostasis: platelet aggregation/degranulation and Factor XII (Hageman factor) form a fibrin clot, followed by fibrinolysis allowing cell migration[cite: 441]. 2. Acute Inflammatory Phase (3–4 days): capillary permeability, complement activation, neutrophil peak (24–48 hrs), macrophage/lymphocyte arrival, and early granulation[cite: 441, 442]. 3. Proliferative Phase: fibroblasts secrete collagen forming pink, vascular, friable granulation tissue alongside surface epithelialization[cite: 442]. 4. Acute Remodelling: the longest phase, where myofibroblasts contract wound edges and collagen remodels into a mature scar regaining ~80% tensile strength[cite: 442].

saqs.question: Contrast the biochemical characteristics of acute versus chronic wounds and list four factors that delay wound healing.
saqs.answer: Acute wounds have low inflammatory cytokines, low matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), high cell mitosis, increased growth factors, and rapid cell responses, whereas chronic wounds have high inflammatory cytokines, high MMPs, low cell mitosis, decreased response to growth factors, and senescent cells[cite: 444]. Four factors delaying wound healing are local tissue ischemia and neuropathy, tissue necrosis and infection, uncontrolled periwound edema, and malnutrition (others include wound instability and poor venous return)[cite: 444].
